game.title: Card sum
game.description: A custom deck of 13 cards is shuffled: 4 cards worth 2, 3 cards worth 10, 4 cards worth 13, 2 cards worth 14. 3 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of the dealt cards' values.

info.raw:
Expected sum ≈ 27.2 (sd ≈ 7.8), and the distribution is lumpy. Informed traders gain a lot from wrong prices, so I quote wide. Each side's width roughly maximises noise profit minus the loss to informed traders.

{"bid": 16.9, "ask": 37.1}

Fair value is about 27.3. The deck averages about 9.08 per card, so three cards average 27.23. The last no-trade nudges this up slightly. The sum's standard deviation is about 7.8.

I checked possible quotes against the two kinds of counterparty:

- **Inner quotes lose money.** Informed traders take quotes near fair value, and the trades we win from noise traders don't cover those losses.
- **Ask:** an ask near 34–35 roughly breaks even.
- **Bid:** a bid near 18 roughly breaks even, because the low tail (sums of 6, 14, 17, 18) is heavy.

So I'll quote wide.

{"bid": 18.0, "ask": 35.0}

Card 1 = 13. Fair value is **30.5**, so I quote **bid 24.9 / ask 38.9**.

**Fair value**

The remaining 12 cards are 4×2, 3×10, 3×13 and 2×14. They sum to 105, so each averages 8.75. The two unseen cards add 17.5 on average, giving 13 + 17.5 = 30.5.

**Settlement distribution**

There are 66 equally likely pairs for the two unseen cards. Adding the 13 gives these settlement values (number of pairs in brackets):

| Settlement | 17 | 25 | 28 | 29 | 33 | 36 | 37 | 39 | 40 | 41 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pairs | 6 | 12 | 12 | 8 | 3 | 9 | 6 | 3 | 6 | 1 |

**Choosing each side**

For each candidate price, the expected profit adds two halves:
- **Noise trader (half the time):** gain = (chance its valuation crosses my price) × (distance from 30.5). Its valuation is 30.5 plus noise with standard deviation 5.8.
- **Informed trader (half the time):** average loss when the true value is beyond my price.

Ask side:

| Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 35.9 | about 0.12 |
| 36.9 | about 0.21 |
| 38.9 | about 0.24 (best) |
| 39.9 | about 0.23 |

At 38.9 the informed trader only buys when the value is 39 or more, which is 10 of 66 outcomes.

Bid side:

| Bid | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 25.1 | about 0.10 |
| 24.9 | about 0.22 (best) |
| 23 | about 0.19 |
| 17.1 | about 0.07 |

At 24.9 the informed trader only sells when the value is 17. The bid stays just under the cluster of 12 outcomes at 25.

{"bid": 24.9, "ask": 38.9}

Card 1 is 13, so about 36.8 is my fair value after the buy at 38.9. I'm quoting a bid of 27 and an ask of 41.

**Fair value with no trades.** The 12 cards left are four 2s, three 10s, three 13s and two 14s. The two hidden cards average 17.5, so the expected sum is 13 + 17.5 = 30.5.

**Effect of the buy at 38.9.**
- An informed trader only buys at 38.9 if the sum is 39, 40 or 41.
- A noise trader values the contract at 30.5 plus noise with standard deviation 5.8. It buys at 38.9 only about 7.4% of the time.
- Updating on that buy puts about 72% of the weight on sums of 39 to 41. The new fair value is about 36.75.

**Ask side.**
- At 38.9, informed buyers mostly hold sums of 39 to 41, averaging about 39.8. That roughly cancels the gain from noise buyers.
- At 41.0, an informed trader never buys at a loss to me. Noise buyers still lift it about 23% of the time, for an edge of about 4.25.
- 41.0 gives the highest expected profit, about +0.49 per quote.

**Bid side.**
- Informed sellers would hold sums of 33 or less, often around 25. That makes a tight bid lose money.
- A bid around 26 to 30 roughly breaks even, so 27 is a cheap way to catch a low noise seller.

{"bid": 27.0, "ask": 41.0}

I'm pricing the contract at about 36.7, which is above where I'm short, so I'll bid 28 and ask 41.

**What's left.** Cards 1 and 2 are both 13, so the settlement is 26 plus card 3. The 11 unseen cards are four 2s, three 10s, two 13s and two 14s. That gives four possible settlements:

| Card 3 | Settlement | Prior probability |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | 28 | 4/11 |
| 10 | 36 | 3/11 |
| 13 | 39 | 2/11 |
| 14 | 40 | 2/11 |

On the cards alone, the expected settlement is about 34.4.

**What the trading history adds.**
- **Quote 3 (buy at 38.9):** An informed trader buys there only if the settlement is 39 or 40. A noise trader buys with only about 7% probability. So this buy strongly favours card 3 being 13 or 14.
- **Quote 4 (buy at 41):** The maximum possible settlement is 41, so an informed trader would never buy at 41. That buy must have come from a noise trader and tells us nothing about card 3.
- **Quote 2 (no trade at 18/35):** A settlement of 36 is above my ask of 35, so an informed trader would have bought. That makes 36 less likely.
- **Stage 1 no trades:** These make 39 and 40 somewhat less likely, but this is outweighed by quote 3.

Putting this together, the posterior is roughly:
- 28: 22%
- 36: 8%
- 39: 35%
- 40: 35%

The expected settlement is about 36.7. I'm short 2, so on this estimate my position is under water.

**Choosing the quote.**
- **Ask:** Any ask below 40 gets picked off by an informed trader whenever the settlement is 39 or 40. At 41, only noise traders buy, and each sale earns about 4.3 over fair. That gives an expected edge of about +1.0, the best of the asks I checked.
- **Bid:** Any bid above 28 gets hit by an informed trader when the settlement is 28. At exactly 28, an informed trader won't sell, and noise sells still earn about 8.7 over fair. That gives an expected edge of about +0.3, better than the higher bids I checked. A buy would also reduce my short.

{"bid": 28, "ask": 41}

The contract settles at 26 plus card 3. The 11 cards left in the deck are four 2s, three 10s, two 13s and two 14s.

**What the trade history says about card 3:**
- **Quote 3 (buy at my 38.9 ask):** Public fair value then was about 30.5, so a noise trader buys above 38.9 only about 7.4% of the time. An informed trader buys only if the total is 39 or more, which now means card 3 is 13 or 14. That makes 13 or 14 roughly 14.5 times as likely as 2 or 10.
- **Quote 4 (buy at 41):** No total can exceed 41, so this was a noise trader and tells me nothing about card 3.
- **Quote 5:** No trade, and it tells me little.

**Updated odds and fair value:**

| Card 3 | Probability | Settlement |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | about 6% | 28 |
| 10 | about 5% | 36 |
| 13 | about 45% | 39 |
| 14 | about 45% | 40 |

Expected settlement is about 38.6.

**Ask:** At 40 or higher no informed trader buys, so only noise traders take it. Expected gain per quote is about 0.41 at 41, 0.47 at 42 and 0.49 at 43. If the market hasn't fully priced in the history, buyers at 43 become rare, so I'll set the ask at 42.

**Bid:** A bid above 28 or 36 loses to informed sellers holding those totals, but those are only about 11% likely. Expected net is about 0.27 at 35, 0.31 at 34 and 0.31 at 33, so I'll bid 34.

{"bid": 34, "ask": 42}

game.title: Card sum
game.description: A custom deck of 13 cards is shuffled: 1 card worth 1, 4 cards worth 2, 3 cards worth 3, 1 card worth 5, 1 card worth 11, 3 cards worth 14. 3 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of the dealt cards' values.

info.raw:
Quoting wide (bid 5, ask 35) because any tighter spread loses money to informed traders at this stage.

- **Expected value.** The 13 cards sum to 76, so the expected 3-card sum is 3 × 76/13 ≈ 17.5.
- **Two-sided risk.** The value depends mostly on how many of the 4 high cards (11, 14, 14, 14) are dealt:

| High cards dealt | Probability | Typical sum |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 29% | about 7.7 |
| 1 | 50% | about 18.4 |
| 2 | 19% | about 29 |
| 3 | 1% | about 40 |

  This leaves large tails on both sides, which informed traders can pick off.
- **Tighter quotes lose.** Bid 13 / ask 22 loses about 0.56 per quote. Bid 10 / ask 26 roughly breaks even.
- **Wide quote.** At bid 5 / ask 35, informed traders almost never trade against me, and noise trades are rare but profitable. I'll keep the risk small and wait for the card reveals.

{"bid": 5, "ask": 35}

The deck is bimodal. 4 of the 13 cards are high (11, 14, 14, 14) and 9 are low (1, 2, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 5).

**Fair value**
- Mean card value is 76/13 ≈ 5.85, so the expected sum of 3 cards is about 17.5.
- The number of high cards dealt (k) drives the outcome:

| High cards dealt (k) | Probability | Typical sum |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 29% | about 7.7 |
| 1 | 50% | about 18.4 |
| 2 | 19% | about 29 |
| 3 | 1.4% | about 40 |

**Bid side**
- The lowest possible sum is 5 (cards 1, 2, 2).
- At a bid of about 7–8, informed traders can only sell to me when the sum is 5, 6 or 7, so my losses to them are small.
- Noise traders (fair value 17.5, standard deviation 6) sell to me there about 4–5% of the time, at a profit of about 10 per unit.
- Expected profit at that bid is roughly +0.15 per quote.

**Ask side**
- Informed traders lose me money whenever two or more high cards are dealt.
- Any ask from about 28 to 32 comes out roughly breakeven, so I quote 30.

{"bid": 7.5, "ask": 30}

Card 1 is a 5, so 12 cards remain: 1, four 2s, three 3s, 11, and three 14s. These sum to 71.
- The expected sum of the two hidden cards is 2 × 71/12 ≈ 11.83.
- The public fair value is therefore about 5 + 11.83 ≈ 16.83.

The settlement value is spread across three separate clusters:

| Pair of hidden cards | Pairs (of 66) | Settlement value |
|---|---|---|
| Two small cards | 28 | 8–11 |
| One small, one big | 32 | 17–22 |
| Two big cards | 6 | 27–33 |

**Bid.** An informed trader only sells to me if the value is below my bid. At a bid of about 9.4, that happens only when the value is 8 or 9, and the loss per trade is small. A noise trader sells below 9.4 about 11% of the time, gaining me roughly 7.4 per trade. Expected edge is about +0.3 per quote.

**Ask.** An ask of 22.1 sits just above the top of the middle cluster. An informed trader only buys if the value is 27–33, which happens in 6 of 66 cases, at an average value of about 31.5. A noise trader buys above 22.1 about 19% of the time, gaining me about 5.3 per trade. Expected edge is slightly positive.

{"bid": 9.4, "ask": 22.1}

Card 1 is a 5, so the true value is 5 plus two cards from the remaining 12. My fair value is about **17.0**, and I'll quote **10.0 / 22.0**.

**Possible totals.** The remaining cards are 1, four 2s, three 3s, one 11 and three 14s. Out of 66 possible pairs, the total lands in three clusters:
- **8 to 11:** 28 pairs.
- **17 to 22:** 32 pairs.
- **30 or 33:** 6 pairs.

**Fair value.** Before any trading, the expected total is about 16.83. At quote 3 nobody traded at 9.4 / 22.1. That is more likely if the total lies inside that range, where an informed trader would have no reason to trade. Updating on this moves the fair value to about **17.0**.

**Bid side.** An informed seller only hits my bid if the total is strictly below it. At a bid of 10.0, only totals of 8 or 9 can sell to me, and those are a small, already discounted share. Noise sellers, valuing around 17 with noise of 6, still sell often enough to pay. The expected edge is about +0.36 per quote, roughly the best bid I tested.

**Ask side.** At 22.0, a total of exactly 22 does not buy, because a buyer needs a valuation above my ask. Only totals of 30 or 33 (about 4.5% of the weight) would lift me. Noise buyers again make up for this, for an expected edge of about +0.29.

{"bid": 10.0, "ask": 22.0}

With card 1 = 5 and card 2 = 3 revealed, 8 is locked in. The contract settles at 8 plus card 3.

**Card 3 distribution.** Eleven cards remain in the deck:

| Card 3 value | Count | Probability | Settlement |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1 | 1/11 | 9 |
| 2 | 4 | 4/11 | 10 |
| 3 | 2 | 2/11 | 11 |
| 11 | 1 | 1/11 | 19 |
| 14 | 3 | 3/11 | 22 |

The expected value of card 3 is 68/11 ≈ 6.18, so public fair value ≈ 14.18. This assumes the earlier no-trade quotes carried no information.

**Ask.** If the ask is just under 22, informed buyers come in whenever settlement is 22, so any ask below 22 takes that loss. At 22 the informed buyer never trades. A noise buyer trades about 9.7% of the time and earns me about 7.8 each time. That gives an expected value of about +0.38, the best of the levels checked:
- 21.9: about +0.37
- 23: about +0.31
- 18.9: about +0.08

**Bid.** Around 9.5, the informed seller only hits me when settlement is 9, which costs about 0.02 in expectation. A noise seller trades about 22% of the time and earns me about 4.7 each time. That gives an expected value of about +0.49. Nearby levels:
- 9.3 or 9.6: about +0.48
- 10: about +0.46
- 10.9: about +0.23

{"bid": 9.5, "ask": 22}

Remaining cards are 1, 2, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 11, 14, 14 and 14, so the settlement value is 8 plus one of these.

**Possible settlement values.** The value is 9, 10, 11, 19 or 22. Before the trading history, their probabilities are 1/11, 4/11, 2/11, 1/11 and 3/11.

**What the history tells me.** No one traded at quotes 3, 4 or 5. An informed trader holding a 9 would have sold at those bids (9.4, 10 and 9.5), so the 9 is now very unlikely. Updating on this gives a fair value of about 14.6.

**Ask side.**
- At an ask of 22, an informed holder of 22 does not buy, because it only buys strictly above the ask.
- Noise buyers above 22 still give an expected gain of about 0.40.
- Lower asks let the informed 19s and 22s buy from me, and that costs more than the extra noise flow brings in.

**Bid side.**
- At a bid of 10, an informed holder of 10 does not sell, and the 9 is nearly ruled out.
- Noise sellers give an expected gain of about 0.5.
- A bid of 11 or higher invites informed selling from the 10s, which carry about 0.4 of the probability, and that is worse.

{"bid": 10, "ask": 22}

info.raw:
Quote bid 7.5 and ask 20.5.

**Settlement distribution.** The deck averages 51/11 ≈ 4.64 per card, so the expected sum of three cards is about 13.9. What matters most is how many 11s are dealt:

| 1 | 0.51 | 15.5 | 13 to 17 |

**Choosing the bid.** The same comparison on the low side gives a net edge of about +0.50 for any bid from 7 to 8. So 7.5 is a good bid.

|---|---|---|

  - 0 elevens: about 0.22
  - 1 eleven: about 0.32
  - 2 elevens: about 0.44
  - 3 elevens: about 0.02
- That gives a fair value of about 17.8.

**Choice of quotes.** The possible sums cluster in groups with gaps between them, so I place each quote where an informed trader rarely hurts me.
- **Ask 25.0:** an informed buyer only wins here if the sum is 33. Meanwhile I still sell to noise traders about 12% of the time, at roughly 7 above fair. The expected edge is about +0.5 per quote.
- **Bid 11.0:** this sits in the gap between the zero-eleven sums (at most 9) and the one-eleven sums (at least 13). An informed seller only hits it when no 11 was dealt. Noise traders sell to me about 13% of the time, about 7 below fair. The expected edge is about +0.3.

{"bid": 11.0, "ask": 25.0}

The fair value is about 22.2. I'll quote a bid of 16.0 and an ask of 27.0, roughly 6 below and 5 above fair, because the informed-trader risk sits mostly just above fair.

**Fair value before history.** With card 1 = 11 revealed, the other 10 cards are one 0, three 2s, four 3s and two 11s. They sum to 40, so the expected sum of the last two cards is 8. That gives a starting fair value of 11 + 8 = 19.

**What the trades tell us.**
- Quote 1: someone bought at 20.5. An informed trader would only do that if the total is above 20.5, which here means the last two cards include an 11.
- Quote 2: no trade at 11 / 25. For an informed trader this rules out a total above 25, which means the last two cards are not both 11s.
- Weighting the possible card pairs by how likely each is to produce this history gives these chances for the total:

| Total | Chance |
|---|---|
| 22 | 9% |
| 24 | 27% |
| 25 | 36% |
| 33 | 2.5% |
| 13 to 17 | 26% |

- The expected total is about 22.2.

**Choosing the quotes.** For each candidate price I compared the expected gain from noise traders with the expected loss to informed traders.

- **Ask:** this side earns most around 27, about +0.63 per quote. Only a total of 33 would be above it, and that is rare.

info.raw:
The contract's expected value is 3.5 × 3.5 = 12.25, with a standard deviation of about 8.9. The distribution is right-skewed: it runs from 1 to 36.

**Choosing the spread.** For each side I compared two things:
- the profit from noise traders (80%, valuation = 12.25 + N(0, 13)) who cross my quote;
- the expected loss to informed traders (20%), who know the true value.

**Ask side** (net expected profit per quote, from that side only):

| Ask | Net |
|---|---|
| ~20.3 | ≈1.46 |
| ~22.3 | ≈1.57 |
| ~24.3 | ≈1.58 |

The curve is flat around 22–24.

**Bid side.** Because of the skew, the downside is cramped (values only go down to 1), so informed traders cost little on a wide bid.

| Bid | Net |
|---|---|
| ~4.25 | ≈1.66 |
| ~3.25 | ≈1.73 |
| ~2.25 | ≈1.76 |

The curve is flat around 2–3.5.

I'll quote a bid of about 3 and an ask of about 23.

{"bid": 3.0, "ask": 23.0}

Expected value of the product of two dice is 3.5 × 3.5 = 12.25.

I compared expected edge from noise traders against expected loss to informed traders on each side:

- **Bid side:** a bid around 2–4 gives roughly +1.7 per quote. Informed losses there are tiny because few outcomes are below the bid.

**Choosing the ask.** Expected profit at ask *a* has two parts:
- Noise traders (probability 0.8) buy when their valuation, drawn from N(21, 13), is above *a*. I gain a − 21 on each such sale.
- Informed traders (probability 0.2) buy when the true value is above *a*. I lose that value minus *a*.

| Ask | Noise gain | Informed loss | Net |
|---|---|---|---|
| 25 | 1.21 | −0.53 | 0.68 |
| 30 | 1.76 | −0.20 | 1.56 |
| 31 | 1.77 | −0.17 | 1.60 |
| 32 | 1.75 | −0.13 | 1.62 |
| 33 | 1.71 | −0.10 | 1.61 |

- A noise trader buys at 32 with probability P(N(0,13) > 11), which is about 0.20.

So the chance of that buy was:
- about 0.36 if die 2 = 6 (0.2 + 0.8 × 0.20);
- about 0.16 for every other die 2 value (0.8 × 0.20).

Updating on this, P(value = 36) is about 0.31, and each other value is about 0.138. The public fair value is about 23.6.

| Ask | Expected net profit |
|---|---|
| 32 | 1.49 |
| 34 | 1.64 |
| 36 | 1.69 |
| 37 | 1.62 |

| Bid | Expected net profit |
|---|---|
| 15 | 1.42 |
| 12 | 1.56 |
| 11 | 1.54 |

game.title: Card sum
game.description: A custom deck of 13 cards is shuffled: 2 cards worth 0, 1 card worth 1, 3 cards worth 2, 4 cards worth 4, 1 card worth 6, 2 cards worth 12. 3 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of the dealt cards' values.

info.raw:
The expected settlement value is about 12.2, so I'm quoting a bid of 8.4 and an ask of 16.0.

**Fair value.** The deck sums to 2·0 + 1 + 3·2 + 4·4 + 6 + 2·12 = 53 across 13 cards. That gives a mean of about 4.08 per card, so three cards have an expected sum of about **12.23**.

**Uncertainty.** The variance for a single card is 401/13 − 4.08² ≈ 14.2. For three cards drawn without replacement, the variance is 3 · 14.2 · 10/12 ≈ 35.6, a standard deviation of about 6. The distribution is skewed to the right because of the two 12-value cards.

**Spread choice.**
- Noise traders have a standard deviation of 8.9. With a half-spread of about 4, each side earns roughly 0.8 · P(Z > 0.45) · 4 ≈ 1.05 from them.
- That outweighs the expected loss to informed traders, which falls as the spread widens.
- I shade the bid lower because of the right skew: a few high values pull the mean above the median.

{"bid": 8.4, "ask": 16.0}

The public fair value is about **13.5**. I'm quoting **10.0 bid / 17.5 ask**, centred slightly above fair value because I'm short.

**Prior value.** The 13 card values add up to 53, so the average card is about 4.08. The expected sum of 3 cards is about 12.23, with a standard deviation of about 6.

**What the trade at 16 tells me.**
- **Informed buyer:** a buyer who knows the value only buys at 16 if the sum is above 16. That needs at least one 12 to be dealt, and has about a 26% chance. Given it happens, the expected sum is about 20.1.
- **Noise trader:** the chance a noise trader buys at 16 is about 34%. That works out to a 47% chance of a buy if the sum is above 16 and 27% if not.
- **Updated value:** applying that to both cases moves the expected sum from 12.23 up to about 13.5.

**Quote.** I'm short 1, so I shade the quote slightly upward. Noise traders' valuations are widely spread, so a fairly wide spread still gets trades.

{"bid": 10.0, "ask": 17.5}

Fair value is about 10.5. The ask is set wide at 16 because of the upside risk from the 12s. The bid sits at 6.5, below fair value.

**Fair value.** Card 1 is a 2. The 12 cards left are two 0s, one 1, two 2s, four 4s, one 6 and two 12s. They sum to 51, so each unseen card averages 4.25.
- Expected settlement is 2 + 2 × 4.25 = 10.5.
- The two earlier trades (a buy at 16 and a sell at 10) roughly cancel, so I don't move fair value for them.

**Shape of the outcome.** The chance that at least one of the two unseen cards is a 12 is 1 − 45/66 ≈ 32%.
- If one is, the total is about 14 to 26.
- If neither is, the total is about 2 to 14 and averages around 7.4.

**Ask side.** I compared expected profit per counterparty at different ask prices:

| Ask | Noise traders | Informed traders | Net |
|---|---|---|---|
| 14 | +0.98 | −0.20 | about 0.78 |
| 16 | +1.18 | −0.10 | about 1.08 |
| 17 | +1.21 | −0.07 | about 1.14 |

Asks of 16 to 17 come out about the same, so 16 is fine.

**Bid side.** The no-12 case has a lot of outcomes around or below 7, so informed sellers are a real cost there. A bid around 6.5 earns roughly 0.8 per counterparty.

{"bid": 6.5, "ask": 16}

Fair value is about 10.5, so I'm quoting a bid of 7.5 and an ask of 14.5.

**Fair value.** Card 1 is a 2, which leaves 12 cards in the deck:
- two 0s, one 1, two 2s, four 4s, one 6 and two 12s;
- these add up to 51, so each unseen card averages 4.25.

The expected settlement is 2 + 2 × 4.25 = **10.5**. The trading so far moves this only slightly. The last quote got no trade, which tells us little.

**Uncertainty.** The two unseen cards have a standard deviation of about 5.2. The distribution is skewed upward because of the two 12s: there is about a 32% chance at least one 12 is dealt, which would push the sum to 14 or more.

**Quote.** I set the spread around 10.5 and make it fairly wide. That limits losses to informed traders, especially on the upside tail. It still stays inside the noise traders' standard deviation of 8.9, so I keep earning their spread.

{"bid": 7.5, "ask": 14.5}

Fair value is about 11.8 given the revealed cards (2 and 6) and the trading history.

**Possible settlements.** The 11 cards left in the deck are two 0s, one 1, two 2s, four 4s and two 12s. With 8 already showing, the contract can settle at 8, 9, 10, 12 or 20.

**Updating on the trades.**
- **Quote 1 (they bought at 16):** an informed buyer would only do this if the value is 20, so this favours 20.
- **Quote 2 (they sold at 10):** an informed seller would only do this if the value is 8 or 9, so this favours 8 and 9.
- **Quote 3 (no trade):** an informed trader with value 20 would have bought, so this counts against 20.
- **Quote 4 (they sold at 7.5):** the value is at least 8, so no informed trader would sell there. This trade tells us nothing.

**Resulting weights.** Combining these with the deck odds gives roughly:

| Settlement | Weight |
|---|---|
| 8 | 25% |
| 9 | 12% |
| 10 | 15% |
| 12 | 30% |
| 20 | 18% |

The expected settlement is about 11.8.

**Adverse selection.**
- **Ask:** an informed trader only buys if the value is 20.
- **Bid:** any bid above 8 invites informed sellers when the value is 8 or 9. A bid at or below 8 is safe from informed traders, because the value can't be lower than 8.

Noise traders' valuations spread widely (standard deviation 8.9), so quotes set wide around the fair value still trade with them. Expected profit per quote peaks around a bid of 7.5 and an ask of 17. Being long one unit slightly favours selling, and the ask is already placed for that.

| Settlement | 8 | 9 | 10 | 12 | 20 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cards (out of 11) | 2 | 1 | 2 | 4 | 2 |

**Update from the buy at 17 in quote 5.** Before that trade, public fair value was about 12.1.
- If the value is 20, a buy at 17 had probability 0.2 + 0.8 × 0.29 ≈ 0.43. An informed trader buys for sure, and a noise trader's valuation is above 17 about 29% of the time.
- For any other value, only a noise trader would buy: probability 0.8 × 0.29 ≈ 0.23.
- So the chance the value is 20 rises from 2/11 to about 0.29.
- Fair value is now about 0.29 × 20 + 0.71 × 10.3 ≈ **13.2**.

**Choosing quotes.** This is the last quote, so I set each side to maximise expected profit for this one trade. A noise trade earns the distance from fair value. An informed trade loses whenever the value lies outside my quote.

- **Ask:** The informed trader only buys above my ask if the value is 20. An ask of 20 removes that loss entirely. A noise trader still buys about 22% of the time at a 6.8 edge, worth about +1.21. That beats an ask of 17 (+0.85) and 19 (+1.14).
- **Bid:** A bid of 8 or below is never hit by the informed trader, since the lowest possible value is 8. Going lower trades less often at a wider edge, and expected profit levels off around a bid of 6 to 7, at about +1.21.

{"bid": 6.5, "ask": 20}

game.title: Dice/cards count
game.description:
Two dice are rolled independently. Repeated numbers are separate faces.
- Die 1 (4 faces, each equally likely): 1, 4, 7, 8.
- Die 2 (8 faces, each equally likely): 0, 3, 5, 10, 11, 12, 12, 12.
game.contract: The contract settles at 10 times the number of dice showing at least 6.

info.raw:
Fair value with nothing revealed is 11.25. Settlement can only be 0, 10 or 20.

**Value of the contract**
- Die 1 shows at least 6 with probability 2/4 = 0.5 (faces 7 and 8).
- Die 2 shows at least 6 with probability 5/8 = 0.625 (faces 10, 11, 12, 12, 12).
- Expected value = 10 × (0.5 + 0.625) = **11.25**.
- Settlement 20 (both dice): 0.3125.
- Settlement 10 (exactly one die): 0.5.
- Settlement 0 (neither die): 0.1875.

**Ask side**
- Any ask between 10 and 20 loses only to informed traders who know the value is 20.
- Expected profit = 0.8 × P(noise valuation > ask) × (ask − 11.25) + 0.2 × 0.3125 × (ask − 20).
- The profit peaks at about 0.78 per quote for an ask near 18 to 18.5.

**Bid side**
- Any bid between 0 and 10 loses only to informed traders who know the value is 0.
- Expected profit = 0.8 × P(noise valuation < bid) × (11.25 − bid) − 0.2 × 0.1875 × bid.
- The profit peaks at about 0.74 per quote for a bid near 5.

{"bid": 5, "ask": 18.5}

The fair value is about 11.05, and I'm quoting a bid of 5.0 and an ask of 17.5.

**Prior value.** Die 1 shows at least 6 with probability 1/2 (faces 7 and 8). Die 2 shows at least 6 with probability 5/8 (faces 10, 11, 12, 12, 12). So the settlement is:
- 0 with probability 0.1875,
- 10 with probability 0.5,
- 20 with probability 0.3125.

The expected value is 11.25.

**Update after no trade at 5 / 18.5.**
- An informed trader would have traded unless the value is 10.
- A noise trader with valuation 11.25 plus Normal(0, 7) stays out with probability about 0.66.
- The posterior probabilities of the values 0, 10 and 20 are therefore about 0.158, 0.579 and 0.263.
- So the public fair value is now about 11.05.

**Choosing the quote.** Each side earns from noise traders and loses to informed traders who know the value is past my price.
- On the bid, an informed trader sells to me only when the value is 0. Expected edge peaks around 5, at about 0.78 per quote.
- On the ask, an informed trader buys from me only when the value is 20. Expected edge is roughly flat between 17 and 18 and peaks near 17.5, at about 0.79 per quote.

{"bid": 5.0, "ask": 17.5}

Die 1 is 8, which is at least 6, so it contributes 10 for certain. Die 2 is at least 6 on 5 of its 8 faces (10, 11, 12, 12, 12). So settlement is 20 with probability 5/8 and 10 with probability 3/8. Fair value is 10 + 10 × 5/8 = **16.25**.

**Informed traders:** they only ever value the contract at 10 or 20.
- An ask at or above 20 is never lifted by an informed trader.
- A bid at or below 10 is never hit by an informed trader.

**Noise traders:** their valuation is 16.25 plus noise with standard deviation 7. Expected profit on each side is 0.8 × P(trade) × edge, minus any expected loss to informed traders.

**Ask side:**
- At 20 (edge 3.75), noise profit is about 0.89 and there is no informed loss.
- Raising the ask a little further increases profit, peaking around edge 5.2.
- This gives an ask of about **21.4**, worth about 0.95 per quote.

**Bid side:**
- Bidding above 10 lets informed sellers hit me whenever the value is 10.
- Expected net profit is about 0.86 at a bid of 11.25, 0.92 at 10.25 and 0.93 at 10.0.
- So the best bid is **10.0**, with edge 6.25.

{"bid": 10.0, "ask": 21.4}

With die 1 = 8, the settlement is either 10 or 20, and the fair value is about 16.25. A bid of 10 and an ask of 21.5 sit outside that range, so an informed trader never trades. Each side earns about 0.9 to 0.95 per quote in expectation from noise traders.

**Fair value**
- Die 1 = 8, which is at least 6, so it contributes 10.
- On die 2, five of eight faces are at least 6 (10, 11, 12, 12, 12). So P(die 2 ≥ 6) = 5/8.
- The settlement is therefore 10 or 20, with P(20) = 5/8.
- Quote 3 (bid 10, ask 21.4) got no trade. An informed trader would not have traded at those prices whichever value is true, so the no-trade tells us nothing about the true value.
- Fair value = 10 + 10 × 5/8 = 16.25.

**Bid**
- With a bid at or below 10, an informed seller never trades, because it only sells when its valuation is strictly below the bid.
- At a bid of 10, the expected profit from noise sellers is 0.8 × 6.25 × Φ(−0.89), which is about 0.93.
- Raising the bid to 11 gives noise profit of about 0.95. But it adds an expected loss of about 0.075 to an informed seller when the value is 10. The net is about 0.88, so 10 is better.

**Ask**
- With an ask at or above 20, an informed buyer never trades.
- Expected noise profit is 0.8 × (a − 16.25) × P(noise valuation > a).
- This peaks when the ask is about 0.75 × 7 above fair value, so a ≈ 21.5. That gives about 0.95.

{"bid": 10, "ask": 21.5}

game.title: Dice/cards product
game.description:
Two dice are rolled independently.
- Die 1 (6 faces, each equally likely): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
- Die 2 (6 faces, each equally likely): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
game.contract: The contract settles at the product of the two dice.

info.raw:
Before any dice are revealed, the fair value is 3.5 × 3.5 = 12.25. The product is spread widely, with a standard deviation of about 8.9 and a right skew.

Informed traders (35%) know the exact value, so the expected profit at each candidate price depends on the true distribution of the product, not a normal curve. Noise traders (65%) value the contract at 12.25 plus noise with standard deviation 6.7.

**Ask side** (expected profit per quote):

| Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 16 | −0.13 |
| 18 | +0.10 |
| 20 | +0.15 (best) |
| 22 | +0.10 |

**Bid side** (expected profit per quote):

| Bid | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 8 | +0.20 |
| 7 | +0.34 |
| 6 | +0.45 |
| 5 | +0.49 (best) |
| 4 | +0.49 |

Both sides are skewed: the long right tail makes informed buyers costly, so the ask sits high, and the cluster of small products lets the bid sit low but still be safe.

{"bid": 5.0, "ask": 20.0}

Fair value is about 12. The prior mean of the product is 12.25, and the no-trade at 5/20 nudges it slightly toward the middle, to roughly 11.96.

**Ask side.** Each quote trades off profit from noise traders against losses to informed traders.

| Ask | Noise profit | Informed loss | Net |
|---|---|---|---|
| 16 | ~0.71 | ~0.74 | ≈ 0 |
| 17 | ~0.74 | ~0.65 | ≈ 0.09 |
| 18 | ~0.72 | ~0.56 | ≈ 0.16 |

**Bid side.** The distribution has a fatter tail on the low side, so bids are more profitable than asks.

| Bid | Noise profit | Informed loss | Net |
|---|---|---|---|
| 7 | ~0.74 | ~0.35 | ≈ 0.39 |
| 6 | ~0.72 | ~0.26 | ≈ 0.46 |
| 5 | ~0.68 | ~0.17 | ≈ 0.51 |

Wider quotes score slightly higher in these numbers. I'm settling on 6 / 18, which gives up little expected profit compared with going wider. It is also tight enough that some trades happen, which reveals information.

{"bid": 6, "ask": 18}

Die 1 is 2, so the contract settles at 2 × die 2. That means the value is one of {2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12}, each equally likely before considering the trades.

**Fair value is about 6.8–7.**
- The stage-1 sale at 6 points slightly towards a low die 2.
- The two no-trade quotes (1 and 3) point slightly towards a high die 2.
- Updating on all three roughly cancels out, giving about 6.8. Noise traders are centred near there with standard deviation 6.7.

**Why quote wide.**
- The possible values are spread out, so each step inward costs a lot when the trader is informed.
- **Ask:** at 12, no informed buyer ever buys from me at a loss. A noise trader still buys about 23% of the time and pays about 5 above fair, worth about +0.74 per quote. Tighter asks do worse: at 8.1 the expected value is about −0.03, and at 11 it is about +0.65.
- **Bid:** the same logic applies by symmetry. At 2, no informed seller can sell below fair, since the lowest possible value is 2. Expected value is about +0.74. A bid of 4 gives about +0.52.

I'm long 1, so a sale at 12 would also cut my position.

{"bid": 2, "ask": 12}

Die 1 is revealed as 2, so the contract settles at 2 × die 2. The possible values are 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 and 12, each equally likely, so fair value is 7. The no-trade at 2/12 on quote 4 tells us nothing, because no value lies outside that range.

**Ask side**
- Ask 12.1: no informed trader buys, since no value exceeds 12. Noise traders buy with probability about 0.223, earning 5.1 each time. Expected profit is about 0.65 × 0.223 × 5.1 ≈ 0.74.
- Ask 10.1: noise profit falls to about 0.65, and informed traders buy whenever the value is 12. That loss costs about 0.11, so the total is roughly 0.54, which is worse.
- Ask 11.5 or 13: both come out a little below 12.1, so the optimum is just above 12.

**Bid side**
- By symmetry, a bid of 1.9 sits just below the lowest possible value. No informed trader sells there, and the expected profit is again about 0.74.
- Buying one unit would take my position to +2, which is within the limit.

{"bid": 1.9, "ask": 12.1}

Die 1 is 2, so the contract settles at 2 × die 2, which can be 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 or 12.

**Fair value.** I updated on the trade history:
- Quote 2 (they sold at 6) points towards die 2 being 1 or 2, since an informed trader sells at 6 only if the product is below 6.
- Quotes 1 and 3 (no trade) push the other way, since an informed trader would not trade at those prices if the product were 6 or more.
- Quotes 4 and 5 tell me nothing. In particular, no informed trader would buy at 12.1 when the maximum is 12.

The approximate posterior is about 0.19 each for die 2 = 1 or 2, and about 0.16 each for 3 to 6. That gives a fair value of about 6.75.

**Quote choice.**
- **Ask:** At 12, no informed trader can profit, because the value can never exceed 12. Noise buyers then give an expected profit of about 0.74. Tighter asks lose more to informed buyers than they gain from extra noise trades.
- **Bid:** At 2, no informed trader sells, because the value can never be below 2. Noise sellers give an expected profit of about 0.74.

{"bid": 2, "ask": 12}

game.title: Dice/cards count
game.description:
Two dice are rolled independently.
- Die 1 (6 faces, each equally likely): 1, 5, 7, 8, 10, 12.
- Die 2 (6 faces, loaded): 0 (prob 1/10), 4 (prob 1/5), 5 (prob 1/10), 6 (prob 1/10), 8 (prob 3/10), 9 (prob 1/5).
game.contract: The contract settles at 10 times the number of dice showing at least 7.

info.raw:
The contract is worth 0, 10 or 20, with a fair value of about 11.67. I quote wide, because informed traders know whether the contract is worth 0, 10 or 20.

**Fair value**
- Die 1 shows at least 7 on faces 7, 8, 10 and 12, so the probability is 4/6 = 2/3.
- Die 2 shows at least 7 on 8 or 9, so the probability is 3/10 + 2/10 = 1/2.
- Expected settlement is 10 × (2/3 + 1/2) ≈ 11.67.
- The settlement distribution is:
  - 0 with probability 1/6
  - 10 with probability 1/2
  - 20 with probability 1/3

**Ask side**
- An ask of 20.0 is never lifted by an informed trader, since the value is never above 20.
- Noise traders still buy with probability about 0.2, giving an expected profit of roughly 1.1 per quote.
- Asks between 11.7 and 20 lose to informed buyers whenever the value is 20, and the extra fills from noise traders do not make up for it.

**Bid side**
- A bid between 0 and 10 only loses to informed sellers when the value is 0, which happens with probability 1/6.
- The expected profit is 0.65·x·P(noise below bid) − 0.35·(1/6)·b, where b is the bid and x = 11.67 − b.
- This peaks at about 0.93 for bids around 1.5 to 2.

{"bid": 2.0, "ask": 20.0}

The current public fair value is about **7.6**. I'll quote a bid of 0 and an ask of 20, which keeps the informed trader out on both sides while still earning from noise traders.

**Prior fair value.** The contract pays 10 for each die showing 7 or more.
- Die 1 shows 7 or more with probability 4/6 = 2/3.
- Die 2 shows 7 or more with probability 3/10 + 1/5 = 1/2.
- So the settlement is 0, 10 or 20 with probabilities 1/6, 1/2 and 1/3. The mean is about 11.67.

**Update after quote 1.** The counterparty sold to me at a bid of 2.
- An informed trader sells at 2 only if the value is 0.
- A noise trader sells there with probability about 0.167.
- Updating on that sale gives P(0) ≈ 0.458, P(10) ≈ 0.325 and P(20) ≈ 0.217.
- The new public fair value is about 7.6.

**Ask side.** Any ask between 10 and 20 is hit by the informed trader only when the value is 20. Expected profit per quote:
- Ask 12: about 0.34.
- Ask 18: about 0.86.
- Ask 20: about 0.87, and the informed trader never buys because 20 is not above 20.
- Ask 22: about 0.70.

The best ask is about 20.

**Bid side.** A bid of 0 is never hit by the informed trader. Noise traders still sell there about 22% of the time, for an expected profit of about 1.10. A bid of 2 earns only about 0.73 because informed traders sell into it when the value is 0.

The best bid is 0. Holding +1 means inventory is not a concern.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 20}

The posterior favours a settlement of 0, so I quote wide on both sides: bid -4, ask 11.

**What the contract is worth now.** Die 2 shows 5, which is below 7, so it adds nothing. The contract settles at 10 if die 1 shows 7, 8, 10 or 12, and at 0 if it shows 1 or 5. Before any trading, the chance of 10 is 2/3.

**What the trades tell us.**
- **Quote 1:** a counterparty sold at my bid of 2. An informed trader sells only if the value is 0, so this is evidence for a low die 1.
  - Likelihood if the value is 0: 0.35 + 0.65 × 0.167 = 0.459.
  - Likelihood if the value is above 0: 0.65 × 0.167 = 0.109.
  - This moves P(die 1 low) from 1/3 to about 0.68.
- **Quote 2:** no trade at 0/20. An informed trader would not trade at either price in any state. So this tells us nothing.
- **Public fair value:** about 0.32 × 10 = 3.2.

**Choosing the quote.**
- **Ask:** if I ask below 10, informed traders buy when the value is 10, which loses money. At 10 or above, only noise traders buy. The expected edge from them, 0.65 × P(buy) × (ask − 3.2), is highest around 11, at about 1.10.
- **Bid:** any bid above 0 lets informed traders sell when the value is 0, which loses money. Below fair, the noise-trader edge, 0.65 × P(sell) × (3.2 − bid), is highest around −4 to −5, at about 1.10.
- **Position:** I am long 1, so the ±5 limit does not constrain either side.

{"bid": -4, "ask": 11}

Die 2 = 5, so the contract settles at 10 if die 1 ≥ 7 and at 0 otherwise. The prior chance of that is 4/6.

**Updating on the trade history**
- **Quote 1** (someone sold at my bid of 2): this sale is much more likely when the value is 0.
  - If the value is 0, an informed trader sells, so the chance of a sale is 0.35 + 0.65 × 0.167 ≈ 0.459.
  - If the value is 10, only a noise trader sells, so the chance is 0.65 × 0.167 ≈ 0.109.
  - The 0.167 is the chance a noise trader's valuation falls below 2, since the public fair value was then about 11.67.
- **Quotes 2 and 3** (no trade): informed traders would not have traded in any state, so these tell us nothing.
- **Posterior:** P(die 1 ≥ 7) ∝ (2/3)(0.109) against (1/3)(0.459), which gives about 0.32. The fair value is therefore about 3.2.

**Choosing the final quote**
- **Bid:** any bid above 0 is hit by informed sellers when the value is 0. At a bid of 0 or below, only noise traders sell. The expected profit, 0.65·Φ((b−3.21)/10)·(3.21−b), is highest at a bid of about −4, giving roughly 1.10.
- **Ask:** any ask below 10 is lifted by informed buyers when the value is 10. At an ask of 10 or above, only noise traders buy. The expected profit, 0.65·(1−Φ((a−3.21)/10))·(a−3.21), is highest at an ask of about 11, giving roughly 1.10.
- My position limits allow trading on both sides.

{"bid": -4, "ask": 11}

game.title: Dice/cards min
game.description: A custom deck of 8 cards is shuffled: 1 card worth 2, 2 cards worth 9, 4 cards worth 13, 1 card worth 14. 2 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.
game.contract: The contract settles at the smallest of the dealt cards.

info.raw:
The settlement value is the minimum of 2 cards dealt from {2, 9, 9, 13, 13, 13, 13, 14}. There are 28 possible pairs.

**Settlement distribution**
- Min = 2 in 7 of 28 pairs, so P = 0.25.
- Min = 9 in 11 of 28 pairs, so P ≈ 0.393.
- Min = 13 in 10 of 28 pairs, so P ≈ 0.357.
- Expected value = 243/28 ≈ 8.68. This is the public fair value.

**Ask side**
- An informed trader only buys when the value is 13 and my ask is below 13.
- For each ask I weighed the profit from noise buyers (above 8.68, noise sd 6.3) against losses to informed buyers.
- Expected profit per quote: 0.52 at 11, 0.72 at 12, 0.85 at 13, 0.86 at 13.5 and 0.85 at 14.
- The best ask is about 13.2.

**Bid side**
- An informed trader sells when the value is 2, if my bid is above 2.
- Expected profit per quote: 0.67 at 5, 0.76 at 4, 0.79 at 3 and 0.78 at 2.
- The best bid is about 3.

{"bid": 3.0, "ask": 13.2}

Prior expected value of the minimum is about 8.68: P(min=2)=7/28, P(9)=11/28, P(13)=10/28.

The last counterparty sold at 3. That is more likely if the true value is 2, because an informed trader sells whenever the value is below the bid. Updating on that sale gives posterior probabilities of about 0.44 for 2, 0.29 for 9 and 0.27 for 13. The fair value is now about 7.0.

- **Bid:** 2.0 maximises expected edge. An informed trader holding a 2 won't sell at exactly 2, and noise sellers still give about +0.85 per quote.
- **Ask:** the expected edge is roughly flat between 12.5 and 12.9, at about +0.8 per quote. I'll post 12.5, which leans slightly toward selling since I'm long.

{"bid": 2.0, "ask": 12.5}

Card 1 is a 2, which is the lowest card in the deck. The contract settles at the minimum of the two cards, so it **settles at exactly 2**, whatever card 2 is.

Because the value is now certain, holding inventory carries no risk. The informed trader values the contract at 2, so it will not trade as long as my bid is below 2 and my ask is above 2.

Noise traders value it at 2 + N(0, 6.3). For a quote placed x away from fair value, expected profit from noise traders is x · P(noise > x). This peaks at about x ≈ 0.75σ ≈ 4.7.

My quote is therefore centred on 2 with a 4.7 offset on each side:
- Bid: 2 − 4.7 = −2.7
- Ask: 2 + 4.7 = 6.7

{"bid": -2.7, "ask": 6.7}

Card 1 is a 2, which is the lowest card in the deck. That means the minimum is certainly 2, so the contract settles at exactly 2 and the public fair value is 2.

**Informed counterparty:** its valuation is 2. If my bid is below 2 and my ask is above 2, it will not trade with me.

**Noise traders:** their valuations are 2 plus Normal noise with standard deviation 6.3.
- On each side I want the offset x from 2 that maximises x × P(noise > x).
- That happens at about x ≈ 0.75σ ≈ 4.7.
- This gives a bid of about -2.7 and an ask of about 6.7.

**Position:** my current long position of +1 is worth exactly 2 at settlement whatever I do, so it doesn't change the quote.

{"bid": -2.7, "ask": 6.7}

game.title: Dice/cards max
game.description:
Three dice are rolled independently. Repeated numbers are separate faces.
- Die 1 (4 faces, each equally likely): 2, 4, 8, 8.
- Die 2 (4 faces, each equally likely): 4, 6, 7, 12.
- Die 3 (6 faces, loaded): 0 (prob 1/5), 1 (prob 1/5), 2 (prob 1/5), 6 (prob 1/10), 9 (prob 1/10), 12 (prob 1/5).
game.contract: The contract settles at the largest of the dice.

info.raw:
Expected settlement value, before any reveal, is **9.09**. I'm quoting **7.8 / 10.4** around it.

**Highest of dice 1 and 2.** There are 16 equally likely combinations:

| Value | Combinations |
|---|---|
| 12 | 4 |
| 8 | 6 |
| 7 | 2 |
| 6 | 2 |
| 4 | 2 |

The mean of this is 130/16 = 8.125.

**Adding die 3:**

| Die 3 | Probability | Expected maximum |
|---|---|---|
| 0, 1 or 2 | 0.6 | 8.125 (die 3 never matters, since the other maximum is at least 4) |
| 6 | 0.1 | 134/16 = 8.375 |
| 9 | 0.1 | 156/16 = 9.75 |
| 12 | 0.2 | 12 |

**Expected value:**
E = 0.6·8.125 + 0.1·8.375 + 0.1·9.75 + 0.2·12 = **9.09**

**Spread:** The settlement value ranges from 4 to 12, so an informed counterparty can hurt badly. I'm using a fairly wide spread of 1.3 either side of fair value. Noise traders have a spread of 2.6 around fair value, so many of them will still trade at these prices.

{"bid": 7.8, "ask": 10.4}

Fair value is about **9.09**, so I'm re-posting 7.8 / 10.4 around it.

**Expected value of the maximum before any reveal**

First, take the larger of Die 1 and Die 2:

| Larger of Die 1 and Die 2 | Probability |
|---|---|
| 4 | 1/8 |
| 6 | 1/8 |
| 7 | 1/8 |
| 8 | 3/8 |
| 12 | 1/4 |

Next, condition on Die 3:

| Die 3 | Probability | Expected maximum |
|---|---|---|
| 0, 1 or 2 | 0.6 | 8.125 |
| 6 | 0.1 | 8.375 |
| 9 | 0.1 | 9.75 |
| 12 | 0.2 | 12 |

- Weighting these gives E[max] = 0.6×8.125 + 0.1×8.375 + 0.1×9.75 + 0.2×12 ≈ **9.09**.
- The quote-1 no-trade tells us very little, so the fair value stays at about 9.09.

**Risk from informed traders**

- The value ends at 12 with probability 0.4, which is the main danger on the ask side.
- The value is below 7.8 with probability about 0.26.
- A spread of roughly 7.8 to 10.4 around 9.09 balances the edge earned from noise traders against losses to informed traders.

{"bid": 7.8, "ask": 10.4}

Fair value given die 3 = 6 is **8.375**.

**Settlement distribution with die 3 = 6.** The contract settles at max(die 1, die 2, 6).
- **Die 1 is 2 or 4 (probability 1/2):** settlement is max(die 2, 6). That gives 6, 6, 7 or 12, so the conditional mean is 7.75.
- **Die 1 is 8 (probability 1/2):** settlement is max(8, die 2). That gives 8, 8, 8 or 12, so the conditional mean is 9.
- **Overall distribution:**
  - 6 with probability 1/4
  - 7 with probability 1/8
  - 8 with probability 3/8
  - 12 with probability 1/4

**Quote choice.** Each side is checked against an informed trader (probability 0.2) and a noise trader (probability 0.8, valuation standard deviation 2.6).
- **Ask at 9.5:** an informed trader buys only when the value is 12, costing 0.2 × 1/4 × 2.5 ≈ 0.125. A noise trader buys about 31% of the time, earning about 0.8 × 0.31 × 1.1 ≈ 0.28.
- **Bid at 7.3:** an informed trader sells when the value is 6 or 7, costing 0.2 × (1/4 × 1.3 + 1/8 × 0.3) ≈ 0.07. A noise trader sells about 34% of the time, earning about 0.8 × 0.34 × 1.1 ≈ 0.29.

Both sides have positive expected profit.

{"bid": 7.3, "ask": 9.5}

Fair value is about 7.9, so I'm quoting a wide market around it: bid 6.0, ask 10.2.

**Prior with die 3 = 6.** The settlement is max(die 1, die 2, 6), which can only be 6, 7, 8 or 12.
- It is 6 with probability 1/4: die 1 is 2 or 4 and die 2 is 4 or 6.
- It is 7 with probability 1/8.
- It is 8 with probability 3/8.
- It is 12 with probability 1/4: die 2 is 12.
- The expected value is 8.375.

**Update for the sell at 7.3.** An informed trader sells there only if the value is 6 or 7.
- A noise trader sells with probability Φ(−1.075/2.6) ≈ 0.34.
- So a sell is about 0.47 likely if the value is 6 or 7, and about 0.27 likely if it is 8 or 12.
- Updated probabilities: 6 is 0.34, 7 is 0.17, 8 is 0.29, 12 is 0.20.
- Updated fair value is about 7.93.

**Choosing the quotes.** I worked out the expected profit per quote for each side, counting noise-trader gains and informed-trader losses.
- **Bid:** Any bid above 7 lets informed traders sell at values of 6 and 7. The best bid is around 6.0, with expected profit about 0.35.
- **Ask:** Any ask between 8 and 12 is bought by informed traders only when the value is 12. The best ask is about 10.0–10.5, with expected profit about 0.27.
- I'm slightly long, so I lean the ask a little lower to 10.2.

{"bid": 6.0, "ask": 10.2}

Die 1 is 8 and die 3 is 6, so the settlement is 8 unless die 2 shows 12. That gives 12 with probability 1/4 and 8 with probability 3/4, so the fair value is 9.

**Ask side.** An informed trader buys only when the value is 12. Noise traders value the contract at 9 plus noise with standard deviation 2.6. The expected profit is:

0.8·P(noise > a)·(a−9) − 0.05·(12−a)

This peaks at about 0.31 for an ask between 11.4 and 11.5.

**Bid side.** An informed trader sells only when the value is 8. Any bid at or below 8 takes no loss from them. The noise-trader profit, 0.8·P(noise < b)·(9−b), peaks at about 0.35 for a bid near 7.0.

Each side is worth about 0.3 per quote in expectation.

{"bid": 7.0, "ask": 11.5}

Die 1 = 8 and die 3 = 6, so the contract settles at 8 unless die 2 shows 12.
- Die 2 is 12 with probability 1/4, giving a settlement of 12.
- Die 2 is 4, 6 or 7 with probability 3/4, giving a settlement of 8.
- Expected value is 0.25 × 12 + 0.75 × 8 = 9.

**Ask side.** An informed trader buys only when the value is 12. Setting the ask about 2.5 above fair (11.5) gives the best balance:
- Noise traders buying above fair: 0.8 × P(noise > 2.5) × 2.5 ≈ 0.336.
- Informed traders buying at 12: 0.05 × (−0.5) ≈ −0.025.
- Net expected profit ≈ 0.31.

**Bid side.** An informed trader sells only if the value of 8 is below my bid. Bidding 8 or lower means they never sell. Expected profit from noise traders is 0.8 × P(noise < −y) × y, where y is the distance below fair; this is largest at about y = 2, giving about 0.35. So the bid is 7.

{"bid": 7.0, "ask": 11.5}

game.title: Dice/cards min
game.description: A custom deck of 12 cards is shuffled: 1 card worth 1, 4 cards worth 3, 3 cards worth 9, 4 cards worth 14. 3 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.
game.contract: The contract settles at the smallest of the dealt cards.

info.raw:
The contract settles at the minimum of 3 cards drawn from 12, so I worked out the distribution of that minimum first.

**Distribution of the minimum** (220 equally likely 3-card hands):
- Minimum is 1: 55/220, or 25%.
- Minimum is 3: 130/220, or 59%.
- Minimum is 9: 31/220, or 14%.
- Minimum is 14: 4/220, or 1.8%.
- Expected value = 780/220 ≈ **3.55**.

**Choosing the quote:**

- **Bid:** A bid of 1.0 avoids informed sellers, because an informed seller holding a 1 values it at exactly 1, which is not below my bid. Noise traders still sell to me about 18% of the time, with about 2.5 of edge per trade. Any bid between 1 and 3 attracts informed sellers holding a 1, who make up 25% of informed traders. That costs more than the extra noise-trader trades bring in.
- **Ask:** At 9.0 only an informed buyer holding a 14 lifts me, which is rare. Noise traders above 9 add a little edge, so the ask has slightly positive expected value. A lower ask, such as 5 to 7, gets hit by informed buyers holding a 9 and loses money on average.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 9.0}

The settlement is the minimum of three cards dealt from 12. The quote is a bid of 1.2 and an ask of 9.

**Prior distribution of the minimum** (out of C(12,3) = 220 possible hands)

| Min | Count | Probability |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 55 | 0.25 |
| 3 | 130 | 0.59 |
| 9 | 31 | 0.14 |
| 14 | 4 | 0.02 |

The expected value is 780/220 ≈ 3.55.

**Update after no trade at 1/9**
- An informed trader would have bought at 9 only if the value were 14.
- A noise trader would not have traded about 79% of the time.
- So the absence of a trade makes 14 less likely, and the fair value moves to about 3.44.

**Bid**
- Any bid above 1 loses to informed sellers when the minimum is 1.
- Against noise traders, the expected edge per quote is about:
  - bid 1.0: +0.23
  - bid 1.2: +0.21
  - bid 1.5: +0.18
- 1.0 and 1.2 are effectively tied. 1.2 gives up almost nothing and fills noise sellers slightly more often.

**Ask**
- Any ask below 9 loses heavily to informed buyers when the minimum is 9 or 14.
- An ask of 9 still makes a small positive expected profit, about +0.045.

{"bid": 1.2, "ask": 9}

The fair value is about 2.7, so I'll bid 0.7 and effectively not sell (ask 9).

**Fair value after card 1 = 9.** The 11 cards left are one 1, four 3s, two 9s and four 14s. The settlement value is min(9, card 2, card 3):
- P(min = 1) = 10/55
- P(min = 3) = 30/55
- P(min = 9) = 15/55

**Update from the trading history.** At quote 2, someone sold to me at 1.2. In stage 1 the public fair value was about 3.55. A noise trader sells below 1.2 with probability about 0.20. An informed trader sells only if the value is 1.
- If the value is 1, a sale happens with probability 0.5 + 0.5 × 0.20 = 0.6.
- Otherwise, a sale happens with probability 0.5 × 0.20 = 0.1.
- The sale is therefore 6 times more likely if the value is 1.
- Quote 1 (no trade) tells us nothing, because no informed trader would have traded at those prices.

Weighting the odds above by this:
- P(min = 1) ≈ 0.57
- P(min = 3) ≈ 0.29
- P(min = 9) ≈ 0.14
- Fair value ≈ 2.71

**Ask.** Any ask below 9 gets bought by informed traders whenever the value is 9. Those losses outweigh the profit from noise traders at every level I checked. So the ask stays at 9, where an informed trader with value 9 would not buy.

**Bid.** At a bid of 1 or below, informed traders never sell, since a value of 1 must be strictly below the bid. Against noise traders alone, expected profit peaks at about 0.24 with a bid around 0.6–0.7.

{"bid": 0.7, "ask": 9}

Card 1 is a 9, so the settlement can only be 1, 3 or 9. Fair value is about 4.27, and I quote at the edges of the informed trader's possible values.

**Remaining deck:** 11 cards: one 1, four 3s, two 9s and four 14s. Two more cards will be dealt.

**Settlement distribution:**
- P(min = 1) = 1 − C(10,2)/C(11,2) = 10/55
- P(min ≥ 9) = C(6,2)/55 = 15/55. In that case the settlement is 9, because card 1 caps it.
- P(min = 3) = 30/55

**Fair value:** (10·1 + 30·3 + 15·9)/55 ≈ **4.27**. Quote 3 showed nothing new, because no informed trader would trade against a 0.7 / 9 quote.

**Ask:** An informed trader buys only if the value is above my ask. At an ask of 9.0, an informed trader holding a 9 does not buy, so I take no adverse selection. A noise trader buys with probability P(N(4.27, 2.8) > 9) ≈ 4.5%, and each such trade earns about 4.7. Expected profit is about 0.11. Asking 8.9 or 8.5 lets the informed trader with a 9 buy, and both give slightly less.

**Bid:** At a bid of 1.0, an informed trader holding a 1 does not sell, so again there is no adverse selection. A noise trader sells with probability about 12%, and each such trade earns about 3.27. Expected profit is about 0.20. A bid of 2.0 drops to about 0.15, because the informed trader holding a 1 sells.

**Position:** I am long 1, so I have room on both sides.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 9.0}

**Fair value.** The revealed cards are 9 and 14. The 10 unseen cards are one 1, four 3s, two 9s and three 14s. So the settlement is min(9, card 3):
- 1 if card 3 is the 1 (prior 0.1)
- 3 if card 3 is a 3 (prior 0.4)
- 9 otherwise (prior 0.5)

**Update from quote 2.** Someone sold at 1.2 in stage 1, when public fair value was about 3.5.
- An informed trader sells there only if the value is 1.
- A noise trader sells there with probability about 0.2.
- So the sale was about 6 times more likely if the value is 1.

The posterior is about 0.40 for 1, 0.27 for 3 and 0.33 for 9, giving a fair value of about 4.2. Quotes 3 and 4 had no trade and tell us almost nothing.

**Ask.** Any ask below 9 gets bought by informed traders when the value is 9, which costs too much. At exactly 9, informed traders don't buy, and noise traders still buy occasionally at a good margin. Ask = 9.

**Bid.** A bid above 1 gets hit by informed traders when the value is 1. At exactly 1 they don't sell, and noise sells still give about +3 edge each. Bid = 1.0.

Ending at +2 is within limits and acceptable.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 9.0}

With cards 9 and 14 revealed, settlement is min(9, card 3).

**Fair value**
- The 10 remaining cards are: one 1, four 3s, two 9s, three 14s. On the cards alone, settlement is 1, 3 or 9 with probabilities 0.1, 0.4 and 0.5.
- The sale at my 1.2 bid in quote 2 matters. An informed trader would only sell there if the minimum was 1, which now means card 3 is the 1.
- Before that trade, public fair value was about 3.55. So a noise trader sells below 1.2 only about 20% of the time.
- That makes the sale about 6 times more likely if card 3 is the 1. Updating gives probabilities of about 0.40, 0.27 and 0.33, so fair value is about 4.2.

**Bid**
- Any bid above 1 lets informed traders holding a 1 sell to me at a loss to me.
- At 1.0 they don't trade, and noise traders still sell often enough to be profitable. Expected value is about +0.2.

**Ask**
- Any ask below 9 gets bought by informed traders holding a 9.
- At 9.0 they don't buy, and the rare noise buyer pays well above fair value. Expected value is about +0.1.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 9.0}

game.title: Dice/cards max
game.description: A custom deck of 20 cards is shuffled: 3 cards worth 3, 1 card worth 4, 1 card worth 5, 4 cards worth 7, 2 cards worth 9, 3 cards worth 10, 3 cards worth 11, 3 cards worth 15. 3 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.
game.contract: The contract settles at the largest of the dealt cards.

info.raw:
Before any card is revealed, my estimate of the contract's value is the expected maximum of 3 cards drawn from the 20-card deck, about **11.98**.

**Distribution of the max** (from P(max ≤ v) = C(n≤v, 3) / C(20, 3), with C(20, 3) = 1140):

| Max | Probability |
|---|---|
| 15 | 460/1140 ≈ 0.40 |
| 11 | 316/1140 ≈ 0.28 |
| 10 | 199/1140 ≈ 0.17 |
| 9 | 81/1140 ≈ 0.07 |
| 7 | 74/1140 ≈ 0.065 |
| 5 or lower | 10/1140 ≈ 0.01 |

E[max] = 13658/1140 ≈ 11.98.

**Choosing the spread:** I tested quoting about ±1.5 around 12, with the bid at 10.5 and the ask at 13.5.

- **Ask at 13.5:**
  - An informed trader buys only when the value is 15 (probability 0.4). I lose 1.5 each time, an expected loss of about 0.2 × 0.4 × 1.5 ≈ 0.12.
  - A noise trader buys about 29% of the time. I gain about 1.5 each time, an expected gain of about 0.8 × 0.29 × 1.5 ≈ 0.35.
- **Bid at 10.5:**
  - An informed trader sells when the value is 10 or less (probability about 0.32, average value about 9). The expected loss is about 0.2 × 0.32 × 1.5 ≈ 0.10.
  - Noise traders give an expected gain of about 0.34.

Both sides have positive expected profit, so I'll quote this spread.

{"bid": 10.5, "ask": 13.5}

Fair value is about 11.98, the expected maximum of 3 cards drawn without replacement from the 20-card deck.

**Expected maximum.** With C(20,3) = 1140 possible hands, P(max ≤ v) = C(n_v,3)/1140, where n_v is the number of cards worth v or less. The counts of hands whose maximum is exactly each value are:

| Max value | Hands | Probability |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | 1 | 0.1% |
| 4 | 3 | 0.3% |
| 5 | 6 | 0.5% |
| 7 | 74 | 6.5% |
| 9 | 81 | 7.1% |
| 10 | 199 | 17.5% |
| 11 | 316 | 27.7% |
| 15 | 460 | 40.4% |

E[max] = 13658 / 1140 ≈ 11.98.

**Quote.** The no-trade at 10.5 / 13.5 tells us almost nothing new, so I keep my quote centred near 12.0. I tighten the spread slightly to roughly ±1.2 to trade more with noise traders. That still protects me against informed traders, given how widely the settlement value can vary.

{"bid": 10.8, "ask": 13.2}

Card 1 is a 7, so the contract settles at max(7, card 2, card 3). The other two cards are drawn from the remaining 19.

**Remaining 19 cards**
- Worth 3: 3 cards
- Worth 4: 1 card
- Worth 5: 1 card
- Worth 7: 3 cards
- Worth 9: 2 cards
- Worth 10: 3 cards
- Worth 11: 3 cards
- Worth 15: 3 cards

**Settlement distribution**

The chance that both remaining cards are at or below a level is n(n−1)/342, where n is the number of cards at or below that level.

| Settles at | Probability |
|---|---|
| 7 | 0.164 |
| 9 | 0.099 |
| 10 | 0.193 |
| 11 | 0.246 |
| 15 | 0.298 |

**Fair value**
- The expected settlement value is about 11.15.
- Two counterparties sold to me in stage 1, which is a mild sign of lower value. I adjust fair value down slightly, to about 11.0.

**Quote**
- I am long 2, so I shade both prices down to make a sale more likely than another purchase.
- The ask of 11.6 sits about 0.6 above fair value, a reasonable edge against noise traders.
- The bid of 9.5 sits wider below fair value, since buying more would add to my long position.

{"bid": 9.5, "ask": 11.6}

With card 1 revealed as 7, my fair value is about 11.1. I'm long 2, so I'm shading both sides down a little to make selling more likely than buying.

**Fair value.** Card 1 is 7, so the contract settles at max(7, card 2, card 3). Card 2 and card 3 are drawn from the remaining 19 cards. The table below shows the chance that neither of the two draws is above each value.

| Value | Cards at or below it (of 19) | P(both draws at or below it) |
|---|---|---|
| 7 | 8 | 56/342 ≈ 0.164 |
| 9 | 10 | 90/342 ≈ 0.263 |
| 10 | 13 | 156/342 ≈ 0.456 |
| 11 | 16 | 240/342 ≈ 0.702 |
| 15 | 19 | 1 |

This gives these settlement probabilities:
- 7: 0.164
- 9: 0.099
- 10: 0.193
- 11: 0.246
- 15: 0.298

The expected value is about **11.15**.

**Quote.** Quote 4 at 9.5 / 11.6 didn't trade, which tells us little. A 30% chance of settling at 15 means informed buyers are a real risk above about 11. Being long 2 also argues for skewing down. I'll put a slightly lower bid and the ask a bit above fair.

{"bid": 9.4, "ask": 11.8}

Fair value after the reveal and the trades is about **11.5**. I'm quoting a 10.2 bid and a 12.6 ask, roughly symmetric around fair with a tiny tilt to sell because I'm long 1.

**Value given card 1 = 7.** The other 19 cards are 3×3, 1×4, 1×5, 3×7, 2×9, 3×10, 3×11 and 3×15. Two of them are dealt, and the contract settles at the highest of the three.

| Settlement | Probability |
|---|---|
| 7 | 28/171 |
| 9 | 17/171 |
| 10 | 33/171 |
| 11 | 42/171 |
| 15 | 51/171 |

The expected value from this alone is about 11.15.

**Adjusting for the stage-2 trades:**
- **Quote 4, no trade at 9.5 / 11.6.** An informed trader would stay out only if the value is 10 or 11, so those outcomes become more likely.
- **Quote 5, a buy at 11.8.** An informed trader buys only if the value is 15, so 15 becomes more likely.
- Combining both, the probability-weighted expected value is about **11.47**.

**Quote.** I keep the spread wide because about 30% of outcomes are 15. I'm long 1, so I lean slightly toward selling.

{"bid": 10.2, "ask": 12.6}

Fair value now that card 1 = 7 and card 2 = 5 are revealed:

- **Remaining 18 cards:** three 3s, one 4, three 7s, two 9s, three 10s, three 11s and three 15s.
- **Settlement** is max(7, card 3):
  - It is 7 with probability 7/18 (card 3 is 7 or lower).
  - Otherwise it is 9 (2/18), 10 (3/18), 11 (3/18) or 15 (3/18).
- **Expected value** = (49 + 18 + 30 + 33 + 45) / 18 = 175/18 ≈ **9.72**.

**Ask side:** At 11.1 or above, an informed trader only buys when the value is 15. At about 12.0, my expected profit per quote is roughly +0.27. That is about +0.37 from noise traders, who buy with probability about 0.20 and pay a premium of about 2.28. It is offset by about 0.10 lost to informed traders when the value is 15.

**Bid side:** The settlement can never be below 7. So a bid of 7.0 cannot lose to an informed trader. Noise traders sell to me with probability about 0.16, at a discount of about 2.7. That gives about +0.34 expected per quote. Raising the bid a little doesn't add meaningfully, because informed sellers start to hurt once the bid is above 7.

{"bid": 7.0, "ask": 12.0}

With cards 7 and 5 revealed, the payoff is max(7, card 3). I'll quote a bid of 7.0 and an ask of 12.0.

**Fair value.** 18 cards remain: 3×3, 1×4, 3×7, 2×9, 3×10, 3×11 and 3×15.
- 7 of them (the 3s, the 4 and the 7s) are 7 or less, so the payoff is 7 with probability 7/18.
- Otherwise the payoff is 9 (2/18), 10 (3/18), 11 (3/18) or 15 (3/18).
- Expected value = (49 + 18 + 30 + 33 + 45) / 18 = 175/18 ≈ 9.72.

**Bid.**
- An informed seller only hits the bid when the true value is below it.
- At a bid of 7.0, the worst outcome is exactly 7, so informed sellers never lose me money.
- Noise traders sell about 16% of the time, earning about 2.7 each, which gives an expected gain of about 0.34.
- Bids between 7.0 and 7.3 score about the same. Going higher lets informed sellers profit when the value is 7.

**Ask.**
- The main threat is an informed buyer when card 3 is a 15 (probability 1/6).
- At an ask of 12, noise traders buy about 20% of the time, earning about 2.28 each, worth about 0.36.
- The expected loss to informed buyers is about 0.10, so the net is about 0.26.
- This is close to the best ask: 11 nets about 0.19 and 13 about 0.23.

{"bid": 7.0, "ask": 12.0}

Fair value is about 9.72, and I'll quote **bid 7.0 / ask 12.2**.

**Fair value.** The 18 cards left in the deck are three 3s, one 4, three 7s, two 9s, three 10s, three 11s and three 15s. The settlement value is 7 if card 3 is 7 or lower, which is 7 of the 18 cards. Otherwise it is card 3's own value.

Expected value = (7·7 + 2·9 + 3·10 + 3·11 + 3·15) / 18 = 175/18 ≈ 9.72.

**Bid.** An informed seller only gains at my bid when the true value is below it.
- The lowest possible settlement is 7, which has a 7/18 chance.
- A bid of 7.0 therefore cannot lose to an informed trader.
- It still catches noise sellers whose valuation falls below 7, worth about +0.34 per quote.
- Bids above 7 add only a little noise flow and start losing on the 7/18 case.

**Ask.** I compared the noise-trader profit against the expected informed loss at several asks.
- The expected profit peaks between about 12.0 and 12.5, at roughly +0.26.
- Above 11, the only informed loss is when card 3 is a 15 (3/18 chance).

{"bid": 7.0, "ask": 12.2}

game.title: Dice/cards min
game.description:
Two dice are rolled independently. Repeated numbers are separate faces.
- Die 1 (8 faces, each equally likely): 0, 0, 2, 2, 3, 5, 5, 10.
- Die 2 (4 faces, loaded): 0 (prob 1/10), 3 (prob 3/10), 4 (prob 1/5), 5 (prob 2/5).
game.contract: The contract settles at the smallest of the dice.

info.raw:
Expected settlement value: 2.175.
- If die 2 shows 0, the minimum is 0.
- If die 2 shows 3, the expected minimum is 2.0.
- If die 2 shows 4, it is 2.375.
- If die 2 shows 5, it is 2.75.
- Weighting these by die 2's probabilities gives 0.3×2.0 + 0.2×2.375 + 0.4×2.75 = 2.175.

The settlement value is spread out:
- The minimum is 0 about 32.5% of the time.
- It is 2 about 22.5% of the time.
- It is 3 or more about 45% of the time.

This wide spread means informed traders can pick off a tight quote. I'll quote a fairly wide market around 2.2 so that informed flow is partly limited to the extreme values.

{"bid": 1.3, "ask": 3.1}

Fair value is about 2.2. If die 2 = 0 the minimum is 0. If die 2 = 3, the expected minimum is 2. If it is 4, it is 2.375, and if it is 5, it is 2.75. Weighting these by die 2's odds gives an expected settlement of 2.175.

The full settlement distribution is:

| Settlement value | Probability |
|---|---|
| 0 | 0.325 |
| 2 | 0.225 |
| 3 | 0.225 |
| 4 | 0.075 |
| 5 | 0.15 |

There was no trade at 1.3 / 3.1, which hints slightly toward a middle value (2 or 3) and leaves the mean near 2.2.

Adverse selection drives the quote because the value often sits exactly at 0 or 5:

- **Bid:** Any bid above 0 is hit by an informed trader whenever the value is 0, which happens 32.5% of the time. A bid of exactly 0.0 avoids that and still buys from noise traders about 11% of the time, at a profit of roughly 2.2 each. That gives an expected edge of about 0.16, the best of the bids I checked.
- **Ask:** An ask of 4.0 only loses 1 to an informed trader when the value is 5. It still sells to noise traders about 16% of the time at a profit of roughly 1.8. That gives an expected edge of about 0.13, again the best of the asks I checked.

{"bid": 0.0, "ask": 4.0}

Die 2 came up 3, so the contract settles at min(die 1, 3).

**Settlement distribution given die 2 = 3:**

| Value | Die 1 faces | Probability |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0, 0 | 2/8 |
| 2 | 2, 2 | 2/8 |
| 3 | 3, 5, 5, 10 | 4/8 |

The fair value is (0×2 + 2×2 + 3×4) / 8 = **2.0**.

**Ask side:**
- An ask below 3 gets lifted by every informed trader holding value 3. That happens with probability 0.35 × 0.5 = 0.175, and each one costs me money.
- At an ask of 3 or more, only noise traders buy.
- Expected profit per quote from the ask:
  - Ask 2.8: about 0.136.
  - Ask 3.0: about 0.188.
  - Ask 3.1: about 0.194.
  - Ask 3.3: about 0.199.
  - Ask 3.4: about 0.199.
  - Ask 3.5: about 0.197.
- I'll ask **3.3**.

**Bid side:**
- Any bid above 0 gets hit by informed traders holding value 0. That happens with probability 0.35 × 0.25 = 0.0875.
- A bid of exactly 0 avoids them, because their valuation is not below the bid.
- Expected profit per quote from the bid:
  - Bid 0: about 0.173.
  - Bid 0.1: about 0.171.
  - Bid 0.3: about 0.164.
- I'll bid **0**.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 3.3}

**Fair value.** Die 2 is revealed as 3, so the contract settles at min(die 1, 3).
- Die 1 is 0 or 0 → settles at 0 (probability 1/4).
- Die 1 is 2 or 2 → settles at 2 (probability 1/4).
- Die 1 is 3, 5, 5 or 10 → settles at 3 (probability 1/2).
- Expected value = 0 × 1/4 + 2 × 1/4 + 3 × 1/2 = 2.0.

Quote 3 (bid 0, ask 3.3) had no trade. An informed trader would not have traded at those prices for any possible value, so the no-trade tells us nothing. Fair value stays 2.0.

**Ask.** If the ask is 3 or higher, informed traders never buy, because the highest possible value is 3. Noise traders buy when 2 + N(0, 1.8) is above the ask. Expected profit from the ask is 0.65 × P(buy) × (ask − 2).
- At 3.0 this is about 0.188.
- At 3.3 it is about 0.199, the maximum.
- At 3.4 it is about 0.198.
- Asks below 3 give up 0.175 × (3 − ask) to informed buyers when the value is 3, which makes them worse.

So the ask is 3.3.

**Bid.** At a bid of 0, informed traders never sell, because the lowest possible value is 0. The expected profit from noise sellers is about 0.173. Raising the bid above 0 means informed traders sell whenever the value is 0, which costs 0.0875 × bid. At 0.1 the net is about 0.171, and higher bids are worse. So the bid is 0.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 3.3}

game.title: Dice/cards min
game.description: A custom deck of 22 cards is shuffled: 2 cards worth 2, 3 cards worth 3, 4 cards worth 4, 4 cards worth 5, 2 cards worth 12, 4 cards worth 13, 3 cards worth 15. 3 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.
game.contract: The contract settles at the smallest of the dealt cards.

info.raw:
Fair value is the expected smallest of 3 cards drawn from the 22-card deck.

**Expected value of the minimum**

The probability that all three cards are at least v is C(number of cards ≥ v, 3) / C(22, 3). Here C(22, 3) = 1540.

| v | Cards ≥ v | P(min ≥ v) |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | 20 | 1140/1540 |
| 4 | 17 | 680/1540 |
| 5 | 13 | 286/1540 |
| 12 | 9 | 84/1540 |
| 13 | 7 | 35/1540 |
| 15 | 3 | 1/1540 |

E[min] = 2 + (1140 + 680 + 286 + 7×84 + 35 + 2×1)/1540 ≈ **3.77**

**Distribution of the minimum**

| Min | Probability |
|---|---|
| 2 | 0.26 |
| 3 | 0.30 |
| 4 | 0.26 |
| 5 | 0.13 |
| 12 or more | about 0.055 |

**Choosing the quotes**

- **Ask:** The main risk is an informed buyer when the minimum is 12 or more. That costs about 8 per trade but has only about 5.5% probability.
- **Bid:** An informed seller with value 2 costs me 0.9 at a bid of 2.9.
- **Noise traders:** Their noise (standard deviation 2.3) is wide relative to the spread, so they trade often. A spread of roughly 2.9 to 4.8 around 3.77 earns about 0.9 to 1 per noise trade.

{"bid": 2.9, "ask": 4.8}

Fair value is now about 4.2, so I'm quoting a slightly wide market around it and leaning toward buying back my short.

**Prior expected minimum.** The deck has 22 cards. P(min ≥ k) = C(cards ≥ k, 3) / C(22, 3), where C(22, 3) = 1540.

| k | Cards ≥ k | C(n, 3) |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | 20 | 1140 |
| 4 | 17 | 680 |
| 5 | 13 | 286 |
| 12 | 9 | 84 |
| 13 | 7 | 35 |
| 15 | 3 | 1 |

E[min] = 2 + (1140 + 680 + 286 + 7·84 + 35 + 2·1) / 1540 = 2 + 2731/1540 ≈ 3.77.

**Update for the buy at 4.8.** The counterparty bought, so its valuation was above 4.8.
- An informed buyer would only do that if min ≥ 5. The prior probability of that is 286/1540 ≈ 0.186.
- A noise trader buys with probability P(Z > (4.8 − 3.77)/2.3) ≈ 0.33.
- So P(buy | min ≥ 5) ≈ 0.2 + 0.8·0.33 ≈ 0.46, and P(buy | min < 5) ≈ 0.8·0.33 ≈ 0.26.
- The posterior P(min ≥ 5) is therefore about 0.29.
- E[min | min ≥ 5] ≈ 7.19 and E[min | min < 5] ≈ 3.00.
- New fair value ≈ 0.29·7.19 + 0.71·3.00 ≈ 4.2.

**Quote.** I'm short 1, so I shade slightly toward buying. A bid of 3.5 means an informed seller only hits it when the minimum is 2 or 3. The ask at 5.3 sits a little above 5, the value in the most likely case when the minimum is 5 or more.

{"bid": 3.5, "ask": 5.3}

Card 1 is a 13, so the contract settles at min(13, card 2, card 3). I value it at about 5.5 to 6, and I'm skewing my quotes so I'm more likely to buy back than to sell more.

**Prior value from the cards.** 21 cards remain: 13 low cards (2 to 5) and 8 high cards (12 to 15). The min only stays high if both remaining dealt cards are high, which has probability 28/210, about 13%. Summing the chance the min is at least each value gives E[min] = 2 + 568/210 ≈ 4.7.

**Update from the two buys.** In stage 1 counterparties bought from me at 4.8 and 5.3. An informed trader only buys if the true value is above the ask, so both buys point to a higher value. I estimated the likelihood ratio at about 2.4, which raises the chance of the high scenario (min of 12 or 13) to roughly 27%. That puts fair value around 5.5 to 6.

**Quote.** I'm short 2, and the most likely outcome is a low value (about 3.5 on average), but there's a fat upper tail near 12.5. So I want to buy back and I don't want to sell much more:
- Bid 4.6, tight enough to attract sellers so I can cover.
- Ask 7.0, wide because selling again would leave me at the -3 limit.

{"bid": 4.6, "ask": 7.0}

I'm short 3, so only a bid is allowed, and **4.0** gives the best expected profit.

**Fair value after card 1 = 13**
- The settlement is min(13, c2, c3), with c2 and c3 drawn from the remaining 21 cards.
- 13 of those cards are low (2–5) and 8 are high (12, 13, 15).
- The chance that both cards are high is 56/420, about 13%. In that case the expected settlement is about 12.5.
- Otherwise the settlement is the smallest low card, with expected value about 3.5.
- Before using the trading history, fair value is about 4.7.

**Adjusting for the buy at 7 in quote 3**
- A buy at 7 is much more likely if both cards are high, because an informed trader would then value the contract above 7.
- Updating on that buy raises the chance of "both high" to about 28%.
- That puts the public fair value at about 6.

**Choosing the bid**
- Noise traders sell to me at the fair-value discount, which helps.
- An informed trader only sells when the true value is below my bid, mainly when it is 2 or 3, which hurts.
- Expected profit for each bid:

| Bid | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 3.5 | about +0.21 |
| 4.0 | about +0.22 |
| 4.5 | about +0.16 |

- Bids around 3.8 to 4.0 are best, so I'm bidding 4.0.

{"bid": 4.0, "ask": null}

Cards 1 and 2 are 13 and 15, so the contract settles at the smaller of 13 and card 3.

**Settlement distribution.** There are 20 cards left: two 2s, three 3s, four 4s, four 5s, two 12s, three 13s and two 15s.
- Settlement is 2, 3, 4, 5 or 12 with probabilities 0.10, 0.15, 0.20, 0.20 and 0.10.
- Settlement is 13 with probability 0.25. This covers card 3 being a 13 or a 15.
- Expected settlement is 138 / 20 = 6.9, which I take as the public fair value.

**Choosing the bid.** I can only buy back, since I'm short 3. The expected profit of a bid b has two parts:
- **Noise sellers:** 0.8 × P(N(6.9, 2.3) < b) × (6.9 − b).
- **Informed sellers:** they only sell when settlement is below b, so this term is 0.2 × E[(v − b); v < b], which is a loss.

Results for different bids:

| Bid | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 3.9 | ≈ 0.165 |
| 4.0 | ≈ 0.171 |
